messages.author: fb5badd8a04823fb
messages.subject: model and distance interval selection
parts:
Good day,

 

We conducted aerial surveys over the Bangweulu Wetlands in Zambia to count Shoebills to derive a population estimate for this species. We flew line transects and counted individuals within a 200 m strip on each side of the plane, estimating the distance of the bird from the transect line.

 

Our data are quite straightforward, as is the analyses in Distance. The outcomes (density estimates and number of individuals) seem as expected, maybe a bit higher, but I have a few questions regarding the outcomes. I hope someone could clarify some things for me.

 

I ran several models at the same time (uniform with cosine and simple polynomial adjustment; half-time with cosine and simple polynomial; hazard-rate with simple polynomial. Do these models make sense?) and Distance determines the best model based on the AIC. So far so good.

 

However, I have selected a few different distance intervals (40 m, 50 m, 67 m) and the interval I choose has quite an effect on the outcome. How would one select between these outcomes? I believe it is the Goodness of Fit with the highest Chi-square p value? I just want to be sure I am making the right choices.

 

And lastly, if I select an interval of 40 m, I get very different outcomes compared to an interval of 41 m. Does anyone know why? Is it because my distance estimates are mainly in 10 m rounding and therefore this affects the outcome? The different density estimates result in quite large differences for our population estimate (15%), which, for a threatened species, could have large conservation consequences.

 

Thanks!

 

Ralf Mullers

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] model and distance interval selection
parts:
Ralf:

Thanks for introducing me to shoebills; interesting looking animals.

I take it you recorded exact distances to the animals you saw in the field, your binning questions relate to binning of those exact distances done during analysis.  That is my premise, I hope it is correct.

There are two places in the analysis where you can perform binning, and for very different reasons.  How to perform that binning takes place in two places in the software and discussed in two locations in the users guide as well.  It seems you are binning in both situations, i.e. binning to assess model fit to data and binning for the actual fitting of the detection function.

Without actually seeing the data, here are some speculative opinions.  If you have exact distance measurements, then you are best to use the Kolomogorov-Smirnoff goodness of fit test that does not rely upon subject decisions about cut points (as does the chi-square goodness of fit tests).  My second comment is if you are binning your data for the purposes of fitting your detection function and you are seeing considerable differences in results, this may be a result of heaping (as you describe); it may also be indicative of other challenges with the data (small sample size, spike in detection function associated with "guarding" the flightline).  With 'good' data, results are robust with respect to cut points.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] model and distance interval selection
parts:
Michelle:

When binning for fitting the detection function Distance will use those same bin cut-points for the chi-square GOF test.  You have essentially asked Distance to ignore the exact distances and perform both the estimation and the GOF with the use of the cut-points you have specified for your detection function fitting.  In your situation, you will need to report the chi-square GOF because, in effect, you no longer have exact distance data.

messages.author: fb5badd8a04823fb
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] model and distance interval selection
parts:
Hi Eric,

Thank you for your reply.

We estimated the distance from the transect line to the observed individuals. As these were aerial surveys, we could not use a range finder, and the distance estimates seem to be heaped around multiples of 50 m (50, 100 and 150). Therefore I choose to bin the data in multiples of 40, in which case the peaks are within the bins. The sample size is relatively small (n = 89), which might explain the different outcomes.

I have the same 'problem' as Michelle Gibson; the K-S GOF is not shown. Thanks for your explanation in regards to this. I will look at the chi-square GOF. Also thanks for explaining the limitations of the analysis and the data set.

Cheers, Ralf
